slides.title: How AWS EC2 Works
slides.subtitle: From a single click to a running virtual machine — and back again.
slides.notes: Welcome. In the next few minutes we'll go from clicking Launch in the console to a VM serving real traffic, then explain the pieces you actually need to remember.

slides.title: The Big Picture
slides.subtitle: What EC2 is, and why it exists
slides.notes: Start with the mental model: EC2 is an API for renting a computer by the second.

slides.title: What is EC2?
bullets: Elastic Compute Cloud — virtual servers you rent by the second.
You choose an instance type, an image, and a network.
AWS boots it on real hardware in a data centre near you.
You get SSH or SSM access to a machine you never touch.
Stop, start, resize, or terminate it whenever you want.
slides.notes: The key idea is elasticity: capacity is a dial, not a purchase order.

slides.title: EC2 in numbers
slides.subtitle: The numbers change every year. The model does not.
slides.notes: Don't memorise the catalogue — learn how to read it. Families encode the CPU/memory/storage trade-off.

slides.title: Under the Hood
slides.subtitle: What happens after you click Launch
slides.notes: Now let's open the box.

slides.title: The hypervisor does the magic
bullets: The hypervisor carves physical servers into isolated VMs.
Nitro offloads networking and storage to dedicated hardware.
Each instance gets its own kernel, memory, and disk.
Neighbours cannot read your registers or your RAM.

panel.title: Nitro vs Xen
bullets: Nitro: near bare-metal performance
Xen: legacy HVM instances
Both: strong VM isolation

slides.notes: Isolation is the product. Everything else is packaging.

slides.title: The instance lifecycle
slides.subtitle: You are billed while the instance is running — and while its EBS volumes exist.
slides.notes: Stopping keeps the EBS volumes and the private IPs (usually). Terminating destroys the instance store and, by default, the root volume.

slides.title: Instance families, in plain English
bullets: General purpose (t3, m7) — balanced CPU, memory, and network.
Compute optimised (c7) — batch jobs, game servers, HPC.
Memory optimised (r7) — caches and in-memory databases.
Storage optimised (i4) — high IOPS and data warehouses.
Accelerated (p5, g5) — GPUs for ML and rendering.
slides.notes: Start with the bottleneck: CPU, memory, disk, or GPU. Then pick the smallest size that fits and scale out.

slides.title: Networking & Storage
slides.subtitle: How packets and bytes reach your VM
slides.notes: Two systems make EC2 useful: the network around it and the disk beneath it.

slides.title: Your instance lives in a VPC
bullets: Subnets decide which availability zone you land in.
Route tables decide where packets can go.
An internet gateway is the front door; NAT is the side door.
Security groups and NACLs decide who gets in.
ENIs give each instance a virtual network card.
slides.notes: A public subnet is public because of its route table, not because of a checkbox.

slides.title: A request reaches your instance
slides.subtitle: Each hop is a policy decision — and a place where things can go wrong.
slides.notes: If the request fails, walk the path: DNS, route table, security group, listener, target health.

slides.title: Security groups are stateful firewalls
bullets: Allow rules only — there is no explicit deny.
Stateful: return traffic is allowed automatically.
Attach several groups; the union of rules applies.
Reference other groups instead of CIDR ranges.
Keep the default-deny posture and open one port at a time.
slides.notes: Security groups are attached to ENIs, not to the instance. That matters when you add multiple network interfaces.

slides.title: EBS: disks that outlive the VM
bullets: Volumes live independently of the instance.
Snapshots are incremental and stored in S3.
gp3 gives you a baseline of 3,000 IOPS for free.
A volume lives in one AZ — copy it with snapshots.

panel.title: Volume types
bullets: gp3 — general purpose SSD
io2 — high IOPS, low latency
st1 — throughput for big data
Snapshots — incremental backups

slides.notes: EBS is network-attached storage. The instance can disappear; the volume can stay.

slides.title: Instance store vs EBS
bullets: Instance store is NVMe attached to the host — fast, ephemeral.
EBS is replicated network storage — durable, flexible.
Instance store is wiped on stop or terminate.
EBS persists and can be reattached.

panel.title: Pick EBS when...
bullets: Data must survive a reboot
You need snapshots
You want to resize or move it

slides.notes: Use instance store for scratch space and caches. Use EBS for anything you would be sad to lose.

slides.title: Elasticity
slides.subtitle: Scale out before your users notice
slides.notes: Elasticity is the reason EC2 exists. Manual servers don't scale; policies do.

slides.title: Auto Scaling closes the loop
slides.subtitle: Observe, decide, launch, register — then measure again.
slides.notes: Target tracking is usually enough: pick a metric and a target, and let the policy do the math.

slides.title: Elastic Load Balancing spreads the load
bullets: ALB routes HTTP/HTTPS and supports host and path rules.
NLB routes TCP/UDP with extreme throughput.
Health checks remove unhealthy targets automatically.
Cross-zone balancing keeps AZs even.
Sticky sessions exist — use them sparingly.
slides.notes: Put the load balancer in public subnets and the instances in private subnets. That is the standard shape.

slides.title: Ways to pay
slides.subtitle: Prices are illustrative — the trade-offs are not.
slides.notes: On-Demand for spiky or short work, Savings Plans for steady load, Spot for fault-tolerant batch.

slides.title: Reliability
slides.subtitle: Design for failure, not against it
slides.notes: Everything fails eventually. The question is whether your architecture notices.

slides.title: Multi-AZ by default
slides.subtitle: One availability zone is a single point of failure. Three is a design.
slides.notes: AZs are physically separate data centres with independent power and networking. Cross-AZ traffic is fast but not free.

slides.title: AMIs & launch templates
bullets: An AMI is a frozen image of an operating system and its disk.
User data bootstraps the instance on first boot.
Launch templates version the instance configuration.
Immutable deploys beat SSH-and-patch.
Auto Scaling groups consume launch templates directly.
slides.notes: Bake dependencies into the AMI, keep secrets out of user data, and version the template.

slides.title: Observe everything with CloudWatch
bullets: Metrics arrive every minute — detailed monitoring gives you seconds.
The CloudWatch agent ships logs and custom metrics.
Alarms can notify, reboot, or trigger Auto Scaling.
Dashboards turn symptoms into a shared picture.

panel.title: Signals to watch
bullets: CPUUtilization
StatusCheckFailed
NetworkIn / NetworkOut
EBS burst balance

slides.notes: Alarm on symptoms users feel, not on every metric that moves.

slides.title: A checklist for production
bullets: Put instances in private subnets behind a load balancer.
Use IMDSv2 and least-privilege IAM roles.
Automate with launch templates and Auto Scaling.
Back up with EBS snapshots and golden AMIs.
Alarm on status checks, not just CPU.
slides.notes: If you remember one thing: make the good path the automated path.

slides.quote: EC2 is not a server. It is an API that hands you a server for as long as you need one.
slides.notes: That shift — from pet to cattle, from machine to API call — is the whole cloud in one sentence.

slides.title: Thanks!
slides.subtitle: Questions? Let's launch something.
slides.notes: Open the floor.
